title: Coverage of changes to the National Planning Policy Framework

content.text: There has been widespread national coverage of the government’s announcement on reforms to the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF), including new measures to support housing delivery around transport hubs and stronger protections for pubs.

The Financial Times, The Sun and Daily Star led on new protections for pubs, reporting that developers will have to prove there is no reasonable prospect of a pub remaining viable before it can be converted into homes, offices or shops. Coverage highlighted the pressure facing the pub sector, noting that hundreds of pubs have closed this year, and framed the changes as an effort to protect valued community assets and support local high streets.

The Times, Guardian, i Paper and Daily Mirror focused on reforms introducing a "default yes" approach for housing developments within walking distance of well-connected train, tram and Tube stations. Reports said the changes are intended to unlock thousands of new homes, support economic growth and help more people live closer to jobs, schools and services.

The i Paper led its front page on the changes, reporting that councils will be expected to approve more housing developments near transport links, including on some green belt land. The paper highlighted examples of locations with significant development potential near existing stations, arguing the reforms could drive a major expansion of commuter towns and villages.

The Guardian reported that the reforms form part of the biggest rewrite of planning rules in more than a decade and highlighted additional measures, including stronger support for development in sustainable locations, greater protections for pubs and support for infrastructure growth. The paper also reported criticism from Conservatives and Reform UK, who argued the changes reduce local control over planning decisions.

The Times reported that the updated framework will help fast-track quality homes around stations while making it harder for developers to convert pubs. The paper said ministers believe the changes will reduce car dependency while supporting housebuilding and economic growth.

The changes were also covered by the Mirror, which welcomed the plans to build more homes near transport hubs and highlighted stronger protections for pubs, reporting that the government is drawing a line against the unnecessary loss of community pubs.
Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner said:
"A safe, secure home is the foundation of opportunity, but too many people are being priced out of the communities where they want to live and work.

"By unlocking thousands of homes around well-connected transport hubs, we're helping people live closer to work, school and the services they rely on, while backing local businesses and driving growth in our communities.
"Pubs are part of who we are as a nation. They're where we celebrate, grieve, argue and belong, and building the homes we desperately need should never come at the cost of the pubs we love."
